insight.title: Why You Add 'Reddit' to Every Search
insight.subtitle: Standard search results feel like ads, so we hunt for accidental human honesty.
insight.notificationHook: Why every search query ends in "reddit"

sections.text: You type a query into Google, immediately hit space, and append the word "reddit." You don’t want a polished top-ten list; you want an opinion from an anonymous stranger who actually bought the item.

Search results are now dominated by optimized affiliate sites and AI-generated articles. Adding a forum name acts as a cheat code, bypassing polished marketing to find messy, unedited human experience.

It marks a major shift in modern internet trust. As web content gets smoother and more commercial, authentic information becomes harder to spot—making unpolished, zero-budget forum posts the highest standard of proof.
We replaced official reviews with random strangers from 2019.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the plain, clear version of today's top news.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said interest is growing for a Black Sea ceasefire. The goal is to protect grain and energy shipments from Ukraine and Russia. The US is reviewing proposals from Turkey and India to move grain. Rubio spoke after a G20 meeting of foreign ministers ended without a joint agreement. Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand said she confronted Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov directly. Anand called out Russia's invasion, stolen children, and ship attacks during a session. She pushed for a truce to protect Ukraine's electrical grid before winter arrives. Anand said Ukraine is engaged, but Russia has not shown willingness to move ahead.

In health news, more than 5,000 people have died from Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Government data shows more than 10,300 confirmed cases across eight provinces. The outbreak started in May and became the country's deadliest in August. The health ministry said the epicentre remains in Ituri province, a conflict zone. The current strain is the Bundibugyo species, which lacks a treatment or vaccine. Violence has disrupted care, and a nurse was killed earlier this week. Kenya has confirmed nine cases, and two suspected cases are in Nigeria. Travel restrictions remain in place for people entering Uganda from DR Congo.

Turning to business, five major tech companies cut stock buybacks by 83 percent to fund AI spending. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle returned 9.3 percent of cash to shareholders. A Reuters analysis shows this is their smallest share in at least 15 years. The five companies saw operating cash flow rise 29 percent to 542.9 billion dollars. Capital spending doubled to 556.9 billion dollars, creating a 14 billion dollar deficit. Alphabet and Meta have not bought back any shares this year. Amazon raised 48.1 billion dollars in long-term debt during the third quarter. The five firms hold over three trillion dollars in future AI commitments.

Next, President Donald Trump said the US is investigating a Chinese spy plot against Nvidia's chief executive. Jensen Huang leads Nvidia, the American company that makes artificial intelligence chips. A newspaper report said US officials found a Chinese executive leaking information to Beijing. The executive worked with a Singapore data firm and had interacted with Huang. China dismissed the intelligence report as groundless speculation. Trump told reporters in Florida that he hopes Huang will be okay. Huang advised Trump on AI policy and visited Beijing with him in May. Trump said he wants to retain Huang as an advisor unless facts show otherwise.

In economic news, American workers took home their smallest share of national income on record. Government data shows the labor share fell to 52.8 percent in the second quarter. That decrease happened while Fortune 500 corporate profits reached a record 2.1 trillion dollars. Labor economist Raymond Robertson said automation is replacing people and shifting income to capital. Worker productivity grew 1.4 percent last quarter while hiring slowed significantly across the country. Employers added 584,000 jobs in 2025. That was down from two million jobs added the previous year. Unemployment ticked up to 4.2 percent in September. Robertson expects unemployment to rise further over the next few months.

Finally, foreign ministers from the Quad alliance called for protecting shipping lanes in West Asia. The Quad group includes the United States, India, Australia, and Japan. Ministers declared safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz an absolute necessity. They voiced concern over arbitrary export limits on critical minerals and goods. China refines about 90 percent of the world's rare earth minerals. To reduce reliance, the US committed 10 million dollars for mineral recycling facilities. The funds will support electronic waste recycling in India and Southeast Asian nations. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Quad leaders will meet in Manila next month.

Up next, five things to know about North Korea's TraderTraitor hackers and a huge crypto heist.

United States authorities blamed North Korean hackers for stealing over six billion dollars from crypto exchange Binance. The October 29 attack is considered the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. Officials linked the group, named TraderTraitor, to North Korea's primary foreign intelligence agency. South Korean intelligence estimated in 2024 that North Korea's cyber force has about 8,400 personnel. Hackers often pose as recruiters on social media to trick workers into downloading bad software. They use the stolen money to buy military parts and build weapons, according to a United Nations report. Federal investigators say the hackers are moving quickly to convert these newly stolen digital assets into cash.

Turning to business news. OpenAI lowered its funding target by ten billion dollars, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The maker of ChatGPT now seeks about twenty billion dollars. Its desired valuation dropped from 1.4 trillion dollars to 1.25 trillion dollars. A tech fund from the United Arab Emirates called MGX expects to be the largest investor. Under the deal, OpenAI could lease new computing space built in that region. Tech stocks fell recently over concerns about heavy AI spending. The Nasdaq index dropped 2.9 percent on Friday. OpenAI set a Friday deadline for investors to commit to this funding round.

In world news, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu won the most seats in Tuesday's election. His political bloc secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset legislature. A rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot took 48 seats. Arab political parties won the remaining 19 seats. The vote created a hung legislature without a clear majority. Leaders are now holding complex negotiations to form a new coalition government. Analysts expect an escalation in the nine-month war between Israel and Iran. Analysts say upcoming United States midterm election results could also influence military decisions. Analysts say President Donald Trump might resume previously paused military strikes against Iran.

Now to space, SpaceX has built the tallest and most powerful rocket in history. The full Starship launch vehicle stands at 407 feet tall. Its bottom booster stage, called Super Heavy, measures 236.2 feet. The booster uses 33 Raptor engines to produce 18.1 million pounds-force of liftoff thrust. The upper Starship spacecraft measures 170.6 feet tall. Together, both stages hold 5,250 metric tons of propellant fuel. SpaceX designed the reusable system to transport heavy cargo and people beyond Earth orbit. For planned NASA lunar missions, the lander must refuel in Earth orbit using specialized tanker ships. NASA will then send two crew members to the Moon's surface and back.

In environmental news, Singapore is testing new building technologies to replace traditional air conditioning units. The city state has the highest per-capita air conditioner ownership rate in Southeast Asia. About 99 percent of private residences are equipped with cooling units. Studies show that building cooling accounts for 40 to 60 percent of a building's energy use. The local building sector creates one-fifth of Singapore's total emissions. To cut energy use, buildings are adopting alternative methods like active chilled beams and radiant cooling. These new systems cool spaces while reducing electricity demands and indoor noise. Singapore aims to lower emissions across its local building sector through these heat-beating solutions.

Finally, Russian oil tankers are adding nets, cages, and rubber tires to block Ukrainian drone strikes. At least 60 protected ships have sailed through the Bosporus strait in Istanbul since August. Maritime analyst Yoruk Isik photographed these vessels during their passage from the Black Sea. Almost all of these ships face sanctions from Western nations for carrying Russian oil exports. Crew members string up nets over engine rooms and hang tires from decks to stop incoming drones. Ukraine stepped up attacks in 2025 to disrupt oil sales that fund Russia's military. In September, Ukraine's drone commander said his forces disabled 300 shadow fleet ships since July.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Many people now add the word Reddit to their online search queries. Standard search engine results are often filled with optimized marketing sites and artificial intelligence articles. Typing a forum name acts like a shortcut to bypass polished advertisements. People prefer honest opinions from anonymous strangers who actually bought a product. This trend reveals a major shift in how we trust information on the internet today. As web content grows smoother and more commercial, unpolished forum posts become the highest standard of proof. It is fascinating that messy human experience has replaced official product reviews. When you search online, where do you go to find real truth?

Thank you for listening to the Sift Daily Briefing, and we will talk to you tomorrow.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. Today we examine the full analysis behind the biggest world headlines.

Could warring countries agree to a small pause in fighting in the Black Sea? US and Canadian officials see growing interest in a limited ceasefire to protect ships.

In February 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. That action started a long and destructive conflict. Ukraine is one of the world's largest producers of grain and vegetable oil. Both Russia and Ukraine rely heavily on Black Sea ports to send exports to market. When fighting spread to sea lanes, cargo ships could not move safely. As a result, food prices jumped for millions of people worldwide. Fuel shipments also faced significant disruptions. To help, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a Black Sea grain deal in 2022. That deal allowed millions of tons of food to leave ports. However, Russia later pulled out of the agreement. Attacks on cargo ships and power grids kept happening as the war dragged into its fifth year.

Foreign ministers from the twenty largest world economies met in Atlanta for two days of talks. The meeting brought top diplomats together to address growing global security problems.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said nations are reviewing proposals from Turkey and India. These plans aim to stop attacks on ships carrying grain and energy in the Black Sea. Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand said she confronted Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov directly. She called out Russia's invasion, attacks on ships, and the stealing of Ukrainian children. Lavrov stated Russia will not accept Ukraine as a security threat. The gathering ended without a joint statement because leaders disagreed sharply over Ukraine. Rubio defended inviting Lavrov, arguing that diplomatic talks require speaking directly with Russia. Meanwhile, the United States approved a two point one billion dollar missile defense sale for Ukraine.

With winter approaching, leaders want to protect Ukraine's power grid from destruction. Nations like India and Egypt also want to protect their own commercial ships and sailors right now.

A limited deal would not end the broader war, but it could help safeguard global food supplies. US President Donald Trump might meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at an upcoming economic summit. Rubio noted Trump could also invite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy if positive results are likely. Listeners should watch if Russia shows any willingness to agree to the shipping halt.

Now, let us turn to a critical health crisis in Africa.

How bad is the current virus emergency in the Democratic Republic of Congo? Government data shows more than five thousand people have died in Congo's worst Ebola outbreak.

Ebola is a rare and deadly disease caused by a virus. It spreads between human beings through direct contact with infected bodily fluids. Symptoms appear quickly and include fever, strong muscle pain, vomiting, and internal bleeding. Congo has fought sixteen previous Ebola outbreaks since scientists first identified the virus in 1976. The country's previous record outbreak killed two thousand two hundred ninety-nine people between 2018 and 2020. The deadliest outbreak in history struck West Africa from 2014 to 2016, killing over eleven thousand people. Scientists developed effective vaccines for common strains, saving thousands of lives during those past events. However, Ebola has multiple distinct strains. A vaccine created for one strain does not protect against a different strain.

A new outbreak began in May and rapidly spread across eight of Congo's twenty-six provinces. By August, health officials confirmed this outbreak had become the deadliest in the nation's history.

Government data shows more than ten thousand three hundred cases have been confirmed so far. The current case fatality rate stands at forty-eight point six percent. Health officials warn this outbreak is driven by the Bundibugyo species. There is currently no approved vaccine or treatment for this specific strain. The epicenter remains in Ituri province, a conflict zone in the northeast. Violence makes it very dangerous for health workers to care for patients. Misinformation has also led to violent attacks on medical teams. A nurse was killed and a politician was beaten to death after promoting health measures. Red Cross volunteers have been injured and an ambulance was burned. Cases have also appeared in Kenya, Nigeria, and Uganda.

The virus is taking lives at a much faster rate than previous outbreaks. Armed conflict and widespread misinformation prevent medical teams from quickly isolating sick patients.

Researchers are running clinical trials to test potential new vaccines against this strain. European health officials say the risk to people in Europe is very low. Watch whether aid agencies gain safe access to conflict zones to contain the disease.

Next, let us look at why giant technology companies are saving their cash.

Why are big technology companies spending far less money buying back their own stock? Reuters reports share buybacks fell eighty-three percent because companies are spending cash on artificial intelligence.

When large corporations generate extra cash, they often return it to their shareholders. One common method is a stock buyback. A company buys its own shares from the open market and cancels them. That reduces the total number of shares in existence. As a result, remaining shares become more valuable and earnings per share rise. For fifteen years, tech giants routinely used buybacks and dividends to reward investors. Alphabet cut its total share count by almost ten percent over five years using buybacks. Analyst Ehren Stanhope noted companies spent heavily on buybacks for over a decade. But building artificial intelligence requires building specialized data centers and purchasing expensive computer chips.

Capital spending by top tech companies doubled, exceeding operating cash flow for the first time since 2011.

A Reuters analysis shows tech giants handed back just nine point three percent of operating cash. That is down from twenty-seven point four percent a year earlier. Operating cash flow rose twenty-nine percent to five hundred forty-two point nine billion dollars. However, capital spending doubled to five hundred fifty-six point nine billion dollars. That left a free cash flow deficit of fourteen billion dollars. Share buybacks collapsed eighty-three percent to thirteen point six billion dollars. Alphabet and Meta bought back zero shares this year. Credit rating agency S&P Global downgraded its outlook on Meta due to high spending plans.

Tech companies face intense pressure to lead the artificial intelligence race. Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy told analysts he sees a clear line of sight to attractive returns.

Investors may need to get used to tech firms taking on debt instead of returning cash. Analyst Ed Yardeni argues that tighter financial constraints could help prevent wasteful overinvestment. Watch whether these multi-billion dollar infrastructure investments begin generating profitable revenue from customers soon.

Next, Donald Trump says the US is looking closely at a reported China spy plot targeting Nvidia's CEO.

Is the boss of America's biggest chip company in danger of being a spy? 

US intelligence officers say a Chinese executive tried to pass secrets about him to Beijing. 

Let us go back to how we got here. Nvidia is a massive US company that makes powerful computer chips. These chips are used to run modern artificial intelligence. Jensen Huang is the chief executive officer of Nvidia. He is the person who runs the company and makes big choices. Jensen Huang was born in Taiwan, and he has built Nvidia into a giant business. He has also advised US leaders on artificial intelligence policy, including President Donald Trump. 

Because Nvidia chips are so important for technology, many countries want them. This includes China. Beijing has been trying to build its own computer chips to catch up with the United States. Jensen Huang has often talked about selling his company's chips in China. This put him in touch with many different business people around the world. 

Then, new information came to light. The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials reached a conclusion. They believe a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data centre company had been funneling information to Beijing. This executive had interacted directly with Jensen Huang. 

Now, this situation has turned into major news. US President Donald Trump spoke out on Saturday, October 31, to support Jensen Huang. Trump called him a brilliant person and said the US is looking very closely at the issue. Trump also said he hopes Huang is going to be okay and that the US wants to protect its brilliant people. When reporters asked if Trump would keep Huang as an advisor, Trump said he would like to say yes. He noted that unless they find something to the contrary, he finds Huang to be very above board. 

Why is this happening at this exact moment? This is happening because intelligence officials recently finished their review and shared their report publicly. At the same time, the relationship between the US and China over advanced technology remains very tense. 

What does this mean for you, and what should you watch next? This story shows how national security and big technology companies are tightly linked today. It could mean tighter rules for tech bosses who talk with foreign partners. You should watch to see what US intelligence discovers next, and whether Trump keeps Huang as an advisor. 

Why are American workers taking home the smallest share of the country's wealth since the government started keeping records in 1947? 

The share of economic output that goes to worker wages has dropped to its lowest level ever. 

Let us look at the background. Over the years, the US economy has grown a lot. Corporate earnings have soared, and corporate profits hit a record two trillion one hundred billion dollars in 2025. The total size of the economy, or GDP, grew three point four percent in the third quarter of last year. 

Yet, the American workforce has not felt that same boom. The labor share, which is the portion of economic output that workers receive through salary and wages, has been sliding. This decade, the labor share average was about fifty five point six percent. At the same time, automation has been growing. Companies are using new computer tools and artificial intelligence to do tasks that people used to do. Analysts at Goldman Sachs estimated that AI automation could eventually displace twenty five percent of all work hours. 

Then, a big change happened in the second quarter of 2026. The labor share dropped all the way down to fifty two point eight percent. That is the lowest level since the Bureau of Labor Statistics started recording this data in 1947. In the previous quarter, the labor share was fifty three point six percent. 

Today, the news shows a growing gap between corporate victories and weak labor data. While profits and GDP go up, employment is slowing down. Unemployment ticked up to four point two percent in September. Employers added just five hundred eighty-four thousand jobs in 2025, compared to two million added in 2024. In September, the US added only twenty-nine thousand jobs, which is about one-third of what economists expected. 

Why is this happening right now? Economists point to a mix of rapid automation and recent government policies. Labor economist Raymond Robertson says automation is replacing people and concentrating income into capital. At the same time, immigration policies under President Donald Trump have changed the workforce. Mark Regets, a senior fellow at the National Foundation for American Policy, says an immigration crackdown has reduced the foreign-born workforce by one point one million to one point four million people since January 2025. This drop happened because migrants were deported or stayed away out of fear. This crackdown did not increase the number of US-born workers as some officials hoped. Instead, it shrank the workforce and made it harder for companies to find the people they need. 

What does this mean for you, and what should you watch next? This trend could mean continued pressure on worker wages and rising unemployment as companies lean more on technology. It could also mean a widening gap where billionaires get richer while ordinary workers struggle. You should watch upcoming monthly job reports and unemployment numbers to see if this trend speeds up or slows down. 

Why did four powerful nations just warn about blocked shipping routes and unfair trade rules? 

Foreign ministers from the United States, India, Australia, and Japan met to demand open seas and fair trade, in a clear message to China. 

Let us trace how we got here. India, the US, Australia, and Japan make up a group called the Quad. They often meet to talk about security and trade in the Indo-Pacific region. Over the years, China has grown its economic and military power. China now refines about ninety percent of the world's rare earth minerals. Beijing has also used export restrictions and non-market policies that create overcapacity, which means making way too much of things like steel and solar panels and selling them cheaply to crush other countries' industries. 

At the same time, global shipping routes have faced huge safety threats. Ships carrying energy and goods must pass through narrow waterways like the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Deliberate attacks and closures in these areas can hold global prices hostage and hurt countries like India, which brings in much of its fertilizer and energy through the Gulf. 

Then, the situation changed at a recent meeting in Atlanta, Georgia. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hosted India's external affairs minister S Jaishankar, along with the top diplomats from Australia and Japan, right before a G20 meeting. 

Today, the news is that these four ministers issued a sharp joint statement. They called it an absolute necessity to protect navigational rights in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. They said ships and crews should pass without tolls. They also voiced grave concerns over economic coercion through arbitrary export restrictions and overproduction. While the statement did not name countries, these criticisms are widely aimed at China and its export curbs on rare earths. 

Why is this happening right now? This is happening because countries are worried about relying too much on a single supplier for critical minerals and energy. India's minister S Jaishankar pointed out at the G20 meeting that disruptions to global oil supplies and attacks on energy trade are a calculated strategy to hurt economies. The Quad ministers also wanted to announce a major upcoming gathering. Marco Rubio stated that a Quad Leaders Meeting will be held in Manila next month, on the sidelines of an Asean conference. 

What does this mean for the listener, and what should you watch next? This means the world's major democracies are teaming up to build new supply chains that do not rely on China. It could mean new factories and recycling plants for critical minerals, including ten million dollars the US committed to facilities in India and Asean countries. You should watch for the upcoming Quad Leaders Meeting in Manila next month to see what new agreements these countries make to secure their technology and energy supplies. 

That leads right into how North Korea's TraderTraitor hackers pulled off a six billion dollar crypto heist at Binance.

How did a North Korean hacking group steal six billion dollars in digital money? United States authorities blamed a group called TraderTraitor for taking the money from cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

North Korea started building its computer hacking programs back in the mid-nineteen nineties. The government trained top students in technology and recruited them into military intelligence units. South Korean intelligence estimated the country had about eight thousand four hundred cyber workers by twenty twenty four. One group linked to them is called the Lazarus Group. They gained notoriety in twenty fourteen by hacking Sony Pictures over a movie mocking their leader. Over time, these hackers shifted their focus toward stealing money from banks and digital currency networks. They stole eighty one million dollars from Bangladesh in twenty sixteen. Later, they launched the WannaCry computer attack in twenty seventeen. In twenty twenty two, they took about six hundred twenty million dollars from the Ronin network. TraderTraitor hackers often trick workers by posing as job recruiters on professional websites. In twenty twenty four, a hacker sent a fake job test to a worker. That test contained hidden computer code that unlocked three hundred eight million dollars from DMM Bitcoin. In February twenty twenty five, the FBI blamed them for taking one point five billion dollars from Bybit.

The scale of these attacks took another step up on October twenty ninth.

United States authorities say TraderTraitor stole more than six billion dollars in digital assets from Binance. Officials believe this is the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The FBI says these hackers move quickly to convert digital assets after stealing them. Much of this activity is run by North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau, its main foreign intelligence agency. A former student said the top two students in his class were recruited directly into hacking units.

International trade rules severely limit how North Korea can earn regular foreign money. Cyber theft lets the country acquire billions of dollars outside normal banking systems. Professor Lim Eul-chul explained that digital money is borderless, making financial restrictions easy to bypass.

Experts say stolen digital coins get converted into regular cash using private exchanges. A United Nations report stated that cyber proceeds help fund the country's weapons of mass destruction. Lim said the money goes straight into military research and buying weapons components. Observers will watch if exchanges can improve software checks to block these fake recruitment tricks.

While security experts track digital thieves, technology companies are facing a different kind of financial test.

Why is the maker of ChatGPT cutting its big fundraising goal? OpenAI lowered its funding target by ten billion dollars after tech investors grew worried about artificial intelligence costs.

OpenAI launched ChatGPT and sparked a global boom in artificial intelligence technology. Technology companies began spending vast amounts of money on data centers and special computer chips. Firms like Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon invested heavily to keep up with high customer demand. Investors pushed stock prices higher because they expected quick profits from these investments. OpenAI also planned to raise fresh money to stay ahead of competing AI companies like Anthropic. It set a goal to list its shares publicly on the stock market in twenty twenty seven. To support its growth, OpenAI began planning another funding round with private technology funds. It initially aimed to raise up to thirty billion dollars from private funds and wealthy individuals.

Doubts about whether AI investments would pay off triggered a sell-off in technology stocks.

OpenAI is now seeking about twenty billion dollars, down by ten billion dollars from its original target. Reports state its desired valuation dropped to one point two five trillion dollars. Some investors reduced their financial commitments before a key Friday deadline. A fund from the United Arab Emirates called MGX is expected to be the largest participant. As part of that deal, OpenAI could gain an option to lease computing capacity in that region. Venture firms like Sequoia Capital, Coatue, and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to join.

Investors are questioning if spending on AI chips and data centers will deliver good returns. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell two point nine percent on Friday. It is down seven point eight percent from its October peak. Chip maker Intel saw its stock drop twenty five percent after reporting weak revenue guidance. Alphabet had its worst trading day ever after search revenues fell short of market expectations.

OpenAI still wants to close this money round quickly to get ahead of Anthropic's planned public listing. If tech stock prices keep falling, investors might demand even lower valuations for artificial intelligence companies. Listeners should watch whether big tech firms cut back on their computer infrastructure spending next quarter.

While technology investors worry about future profits, world leaders are watching a growing military crisis in the Middle East.

Why are diplomats racing to stop a new outbreak of fighting between the United States and Iran? Qatari mediators held emergency talks because regional leaders fear President Donald Trump might restart military strikes.

President Trump launched a war against Iran alongside Israel in February. During the war, Iran's previous supreme leader was killed, and his son Mojtaba Khamenei took power. Fighting damaged trade routes around the Strait of Hormuz, where much of the world's oil travels. Iran blocked commercial ships, while the United States put a blockade on Iranian ports. To lower tensions, Iran proposed a seven-day plan in September to unfreeze assets and open shipping lanes. President Trump rejected that plan, but he paused military strikes during the weeks before the American midterm elections. He urged Israeli voters to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in power. He said they could finish the job together.

With the US elections arriving on Tuesday, diplomatic talks intensified in Qatar and Tehran.

Iranian envoys met Qatari mediators in Doha on Saturday after twelve hours of talks in Tehran on Friday. Vice President JD Vance sent a letter proposing direct talks about Iran's nuclear program. Senior Iranian official Mohsen Rezaei called the letter a positive sign that showed a complete shift in tone. However, President Trump played down the letter. He said it was basically about getting medical supplies to sick people. Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed talks are active, but said Trump has not decided on further strikes. Meanwhile, Supreme Leader Khamenei ordered the military to be ready to respond to any threat without geographic limits.

Governments in the Middle East expect military action could restart as soon as voting ends on Tuesday. Rubio warned that Iranian attacks on commercial ships threaten global food and energy supplies.

If talks fail, renewed strikes could disrupt oil shipments and push global fuel prices higher. Negotiators are trying to arrange a direct meeting within a week, possibly in Doha or Istanbul. Listeners should watch whether both sides agree to a temporary pause before military action resumes.

Up next, we take a look at how big and powerful SpaceX's Starship rocket is.

How big and powerful is SpaceX's Starship rocket? It is currently the tallest and most powerful rocket ever flown.

Space exploration companies have built rockets for decades to reach Earth orbit. Traditional rockets discard their boosters into the ocean after a single flight. This practice makes every space mission very costly to launch. SpaceX set out to solve this problem by making rockets fully reusable. Reusing rockets could lower costs and allow more frequent trips to space. The company designed a system capable of carrying huge payloads into orbit. Payloads are the heavy cargo and satellites carried inside a spacecraft. SpaceX also planned to carry groups of people beyond Earth orbit. To lift such massive weight, engineers needed unprecedented engine power. They created a system built in two distinct parts. The bottom section acts as a heavy booster to fight Earth's gravity. The top section acts as the actual spacecraft for deep space travel.

SpaceX built the full two-stage vehicle and began launching it on test flights.

Today, the fully stacked Starship vehicle stands at 407 feet tall. That makes it taller than Hyperion, the tallest known living tree. It is also one-third taller than the Statue of Liberty including its pedestal. The lower section is a 236.2-foot booster called Super Heavy. Super Heavy uses 33 Raptor engines that burn liquid methane and liquid oxygen. Together, those engines generate 18.1 million pounds-force of liftoff thrust. By comparison, NASA's Space Launch System produces 8.8 million to 9.4 million pounds. Above the booster sits the 170.6-foot Starship spacecraft. Starship uses three regular Raptor engines and three Raptor Vacuum engines designed for space. The upper stage generates roughly 3.5 million pounds-force of thrust. The booster holds 3,650 metric tons of fuel. The Starship spacecraft holds another 1,600 metric tons of fuel. That brings the total propellant weight to 5,250 metric tons. During its first full launch in April 2023, the booster produced 16.7 million pounds of thrust. That blast shattered the concrete launch pad and scattered debris across 385 acres.

NASA selected Starship for its Artemis program to put humans back on the Moon.

Starship must refuel in Earth orbit before it can travel to the Moon. The lander burns a huge amount of fuel just getting into orbit around Earth. SpaceX plans to launch a propellant depot into orbit first. Then tanker Starships will deliver cold fuel to that depot. The lunar lander will dock with the depot and fill its tanks. Astronauts will launch separately aboard NASA's Orion spacecraft to meet the lander. Starship will then carry two crew members down to the Moon's surface. Managing freezing propellants in space is a major technical challenge to watch.

Now, let us turn to a different kind of energy story in Southeast Asia.

Singapore is testing alternative cooling methods to lower municipal electricity use. Long called an air-conditioned nation, it has the highest per-capita air conditioner ownership rate in Southeast Asia. The city state is experimenting with alternatives like chilled beams and passive displacement. This testing aims to curb its high demand for energy-guzzling air conditioning.

Next, we look at how a war at sea is changing shipping defenses.

Why are Russian oil tankers suddenly covered in fishing nets and metal cages? They are using makeshift armor to defend against Ukrainian aerial drone attacks.

Russia relies heavily on foreign oil sales to pay for its war effort. Western nations imposed sanctions on Russian oil to reduce Moscow's income. To bypass restrictions, Russia uses a shadow fleet of aging cargo ships. These shadow tankers operate outside standard global shipping norms and regular insurance rules. Instead, Russian state-backed banks underwrite and insure these unrated oil vessels. At the same time, Ukraine relies on drones and war robots to fight the invasion. Ukraine uses ground robots and remote pilots to keep human soldiers away from danger zones. Ukrainian units use drones to strike Russian refineries, data centers, and military sites. Small first-person-view drones can easily slip past expensive air defense systems. In response, ground forces began placing metal cope cages on military vehicles for protection.

Ukraine expanded its drone strikes to target the shadow fleet moving through the Black Sea.

Maritime analyst Yoruk Isik has documented at least 60 draped tankers passing Istanbul since August. Isik leads the consulting firm Bosphorus Observer and photographed the sanctioned vessels. Nearly all the documented ships were already under Western sanctions for carrying Russian oil. The tankers hang rubber tires, metal cages, and large nets over their decks. Analysts say these crude tools shield sensitive areas like engine parts and rudders from drone impacts. Independent analyst Eric Woods said the netting looks like defenses used in front-line cities like Kharkiv. Ukraine's drone commander claimed in September that his forces disabled 300 shadow fleet vessels since July. That figure has not been independently verified.

Ukraine increased these strikes in 2025 to build leverage while Washington pushed for peace talks.

The strikes aim to strain Russian banks that insure the shadow fleet. Russian strikes on Ukrainian ports have also raised global wheat prices. Analyst Samuel Bendett says nets and cages are the cheapest way to defend ships against drones. He expects this makeshift protection to become a global trend for maritime shipping.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

When you search for something online today, you might type your question and add one extra word. That word is often "reddit". You do not want a polished list of top products from a fancy website. You want an honest opinion from a stranger who actually bought the item. Search engine results are now filled with optimized marketing pages and artificial intelligence text. Adding a forum name works like a secret shortcut. It lets you skip smooth ads to find real, unedited human experiences. This simple habit shows how trust on the internet is changing. As online content becomes cleaner and more commercial, real truth gets harder to find. Unpolished forum posts with zero budget have become the highest proof of honesty. Many of us now trust random strangers from 2019 more than official review websites. It is fascinating how we search for real human voices in a world of automated content. Next time you search the web, ask yourself whose voice you are really looking for.

Thank you for listening to Sift In-Depth today. Stay curious, and we will talk again soon.
